title: From Self-driving to Autonomous Voice Agents — Brooke Hopkins, Coval

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation design methodology—reference-free probabilistic evaluation, CI/CD eval loops, simulation realism hierarchies, denoising, and LLM-as-judge calibration—rather than building any single system. The evaluation framework is presented as broadly applicable across verticals while concrete examples center on customer-facing voice scenarios like call volume, IVR replacement, refunds, and appointment booking. The talk spans the full evaluation lifecycle from pre-deployment module and end-to-end evals through CI/CD regression loops to live production monitoring feeding back into simulations. Prerequisites are modest—familiarity with LLM agents and CI/CD—but the evaluation concepts (probabilistic simulation, denoising, metric calibration) require intermediate AI engineering maturity. A single-speaker industry conference presentation drawing on firsthand experience at Waymo and Coval. Claims are grounded in the speaker's practitioner experience building evaluation infrastructure at Waymo and Coval rather than formal peer-reviewed research.

summary: Brooke Hopkins presents lessons from self-driving evaluation applied to voice agents. Trust is the biggest deployment barrier: companies simultaneously overestimate (automating all call volume at once) and underestimate (scoping too small) agent capabilities. Voice agents get stuck in POC hell because enterprises fear customer-facing deployment. She presents two current approaches—conservative/deterministic (expensive IVR tree) versus autonomous/flexible (unpredictable)—and argues this is a false choice, using Waymo as proof that reliability and autonomy coexist. Self-driving's key unlock was large-scale simulation, evolving from manual driving tests (hard to scale) to specific scenario tests (brittle, expensive) to large-scale probabilistic evaluation (measuring event frequency across many simulations). Self-driving and conversational evals share fundamental similarity: both interact with the real world step-by-step, making simulation essential. LLM non-determinism is useful for coverage. Hopkins contrasts input-output evaluation (golden datasets) with probabilistic, reference-free evaluation (how often the agent resolves inquiries, repeats itself, or says inappropriate things). Continuous eval loops mirror CI/CD: pre-submit, post-submit, regression, release validation, and live monitoring feeding back into simulations. Manual evals remain valuable for human judgment calls. On realism, she advocates a hierarchy: text-only for workflow iteration, simple voices for interruption/latency testing, hyperrealistic voices only for recreating production issues. Denoising—reimulating failures many times to determine failure probability—reveals whether issues are systematic or occasional. She then addresses building an eval strategy: evals are a core part of product development, not just engineering best practice. Companies should think through what their vertical agent should do well and what they don't care about, since different applications prioritize different metrics (latency for outbound sales, instruction following for appointment booking). LLM-as-judge is powerful but noisy; Coval's metric studio lets teams calibrate automated metrics with human feedback before deploying at scale. Her recommended eval approach progresses from public benchmarks to custom benchmarking on domain-specific data, to task-based evals of individual modules, to end-to-end evals at production scale. She emphasizes creating a continuous eval process with monitoring, bug-handling workflows, test set hierarchies, and dashboards. She closes by positioning voice as the next platform shift (web → mobile → voice), predicting every enterprise will launch a voice experience within three years.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Brooke Hopkins introduces herself as founder of Coval, building evals for voice agents. She previously led the eval job infrastructure team at Waymo responsible for developer tools and simulation, and now applies self-driving and robotics learnings to voice agents.

sections.title: Voice Agent Trust and Scaling Challenges
sections.summary: Voice agents have massive promise but trust is the biggest barrier to deployment. Companies paradoxically overestimate (automating all call volume at once) and underestimate (scoping too small) agent capabilities. Two current approaches: conservative/deterministic (expensive IVR tree) and autonomous/flexible (unpredictable). Hopkins argues this is a false choice—you can have reliability and autonomy.

sections.title: Waymo and Large-Scale Simulation as Unlock
sections.summary: Waymo is cited as proof that reliability and autonomy can coexist. Large-scale simulation was the huge unlock for self-driving and robotics. Hopkins traces evolution from manual eval (driving streets, noting failures) to specific scenario tests (brittle, expensive) to large-scale evaluation (measuring event frequency across many simulations).

sections.title: Similarity Between Self-Driving and Conversational Evals
sections.summary: Self-driving and conversational evals are fundamentally similar: both interact with the real world, responding step-by-step to an environment. Simulation is essential because static tests break and manual testing is expensive. LLM non-determinism is useful for coverage, showing all possible responses and computing probability of agent success across many simulations.

sections.title: Probabilistic vs Input-Output Evaluation
sections.summary: Input-output evals use golden datasets with specific expected outputs for given inputs. Conversational evals require reference-free probabilistic evaluation—defining how often the agent resolves inquiries, repeats itself, or says inappropriate things across many scenarios. This is what allowed Waymo to scale and what will allow voice agents to scale.

sections.title: Continuous Eval Loops and CI/CD
sections.summary: Constant eval loops made autonomous vehicles scalable and will do the same for voice. The process mirrors CI/CD: reproduce bugs, iterate, run regression sets, pre-submit and post-submit checks, large-scale release validation, and live monitoring feeding back into the system. Manual evals remain valuable for human judgment—the goal is not full automation but leveraging auto evals for speed and scale.

sections.title: Simulation Realism Hierarchy
sections.summary: Level of realism depends on what you're testing. Text-only suffices for workflow, tool calls, and instruction following iteration. Simple voices suffice for interruptions, latency, and pauses. Hyperrealistic voices (accents, background noise, audio quality) are only needed when recreating production issues. Right-sizing simulation to the testing goal is critical for a good eval strategy.

sections.title: Denoising Tactic
sections.summary: Denoising involves reimulating a failing scenario many times (e.g., 100 times) to determine the probability of failure—whether it's a coin flip (50/100), systematic (99/100), or occasional (1/100). This is more important for agents than knowing about a single failure. Teams should define target reliability levels (analogous to cloud infrastructure's nines of reliability) for different parts of their product.

sections.title: Building an Eval Strategy and Metrics Thinking
sections.summary: Evals are a core part of product development, not just engineering best practice. Companies should think through what their vertical agent should do well and what they don't care about, since general voice models already exist. Different applications prioritize different metrics: latency matters for outbound sales but not necessarily for refunds; instruction following matters for appointment booking but less for conversational roles like therapists or interviewers. Key metric categories include latency, interruptions, workflows, and instruction adherence.

sections.title: LLM-as-Judge and Metric Calibration
sections.summary: LLM-as-judge is flexible but noisy—generic questions like 'was this conversation successful' produce inconsistent results across runs. Coval's metric studio allows teams to iterate on automated metrics and incorporate human feedback until the metrics correlate with human judgment. This calibration gives confidence to deploy automated metrics across 10,000 conversations instead of the 10 or 100 that were manually labeled.

sections.title: Progressive Eval Approach: Benchmarks to End-to-End
sections.summary: Hopkins recommends a layered eval approach: start with public benchmarks for rough direction, then benchmark with your own domain-specific data (e.g., medical terms for a medical company), then run task-based evals on specific modules (not every module needs to be enabled to test one thing), then end-to-end evals at production scale. Benchmarking each part of the voice stack—transcription, LLM, voice—on specific data helps select optimal models since voice involves many models with different tradeoffs.

sections.title: Creating a Continuous Eval Process
sections.summary: A mature eval process includes continuous monitoring, defined bug-handling workflows (who takes a production bug and which test set it goes into), test set hierarchies (by customer, customer type, workflow, or feature), and dashboards for ongoing visibility. Hopkins emphasizes this continuous process is often underestimated—teams should not just check whether the agent works during a pilot period but maintain ongoing eval infrastructure.

sections.title: Voice as the Next Platform Shift
sections.summary: Hopkins positions voice as the next major platform shift after web and mobile. She predicts every enterprise will launch a voice experience within three years, making good voice AI a baseline expectation like having a mobile app. Coval aims to enable this future with integrated eval infrastructure and is hiring, noting the field is technically interesting due to the diversity of models, scalability challenges, and open frontier problems.
